item.title: Griz 10 Month Checkin
item.description:
Griz 10 Month Checkin

As Griz hits 10 months, I wanted to put a few videos together to show how she’s doing.

Working with Kids

Griz being a high energy working line German Shepherd, means she can be hard to handle. Cassius being a 5-year-old child is going to have a hard time managing a dog like her without some training for the both of them. Once a day Cass works with either Griz or Denali to perform some interaction with his dogs. The leash skills are the hardest for a little guy to handle, so when we work on that, I have him choke up on the lead near the collar, we use a pinch or slip collar, and I take the tail end. I give him a chance to administer corrections; however, I use the tail of the lead to give corrections that he misses. For play, Griz has been generalized on long distance arounds, so, that one is pretty easy for him to play fetch with her. Then we work on classical conditioning together as well. He is still deciding on his reward marker, and I’m not too concerned if he changes it too often, because he’s a kid… And also, our dogs are smart enough to pick up on the other classically conditioned signs. If I give Cass food and ask him to work on his reward marker, the dogs are already tuned in because they’ve been through this before.

item.title: The Dog Gear Of Griz
item.description:
Full unedited video

I broke down each piece of gear I use, and why I use it in this video. The subsequent videos are subvideos from this main clip.

Flat Collar

Flat collars are the most common and most useless of the collars. They look nice, but put all the pressure on the throat when making corrections. I still use them on occasion, the best thing I like it for is with tracking. When attached for tracking I let the long lead go between her legs so the pressure is put on the back of the neck instead of the throat. I make no aversive corrections on the track; however, if she pulls into the lead with the flat collar on in this fashion, it will pull her head in the direction of the scent.

item.title: Griz 8 Month Bite Drive
item.description:
Currently going over the Haz’s videos from sheildk9 online. He has some videos in there for building drive with dogs. He refers to it as activating the dog. The idea is pretty simle:

  1. Chase, Reward
  2. Frustrate, Chase, Reward
  3. Frustrate, Obedience, chase, Reward

So I’m taking that idea and trying to get faster sits and downs out of Griz here. My personal frustration is if you look at how good her here or front command sit is, it’s great. But her sit at any distance is slow and rolled back. Her downs are the same. It’s pretty crazy becau her sit in motion looks better than a sit at 5 feet out. But that’s what we are going to work on trying to fix

item.title: Griz 5 Months Air Scent
item.description:
Air Scent

All this was filmed on her 3rd day of air scent training. This training has nothing to do with IGP. If anything, it’s going to make the tracking portion of IGP harder. That being said, working air scent and trailing exercises is a ton of fun, and has lots of practical uses outside of the sport of IGP

In the future

We’ll be getting some better video footage of this next week. We are going on a camping trip where we will start using this training for hide and seek with the kid. And I’ll be taking her out on off trail hikes, dropping the jacket as a marker at the camp site, then having her lead me back.

Sendaway

Griz is getting to good enough where I can start increasing distance, and fading the lure. Denali on the other hand, doesn’t know this drill. She’s on a full on lure. Working this with a green dog might be a little harder than what you see here with Denali, but only because Denali has some experience learning from me already and she understands luring pretty well.

The video is sped up by 300% in an attempt to not be so boring. 1st we have my pup, Griz. She is doing her 1st corner. She probably has the most practice at this drill out of all 3 dogs.

Then we have Argos, Griz’s big brother. His nose is killer, he’s wicked smart and here we have a short clip of him tracking in the mud. His nose is fine but we went to the mud so we could bring his attention to every footstep.

item.title: IGP RULES
item.description:
ruleset

Basic Requirements for dog behavior

  • Confidence
  • Free, happy, motivated to work
  • Attentive to the handler
  • Harmony of the team whatever that means
  • Correctness
  • Acceptance of commands
  • Basic assesment of execution of trial exercises
  • Response to verbal

Verbal corrections

  • 1 additional command is 1.5 deduction
  • 2nd additional commands are each 2.5 point ———-
  • 3rd additional command is a dq for the round

Praise

May be praised after each exercise, must be back in position within 5 seconds

item.title: Bark training 1
item.description: The goal is to give power to her barks. I want her to think she can make me come to her, or make me flee based on her barks. If I ask her to get scary, we want to see powerful barks. To get this we are going to use shaping and frustration with the tug. As she barks I’ll move closer. Initially, I should reward any vocal barks with forward motion and should avoid resetting. As time goes on I want to start getting stronger and more sustained barks. Eventually, this should turn into a game where I can move back or go still, and she’ll bring me to life with barking.

item.title: Bark training 2
item.description:
Alright this is like a week after Bark Training 1. We’ve done the tie back a few times and I think I can get her to do it with me holding her back. This can be confusing for her, and I wouldn’t want to try it if I didn’t think she was ready. And we’ll want to do this a few times before we move to having a helper.

The technique here is shaping again, this time instead of me getting closer to her, we get closer to the ball. I see some guys on youtube using agitation collars for this; but, I want to keep my leash pressure communication strong, so I’m going to use harnesses most of the time.

item.title: Detection 1
item.description: In this video I’m still trying to figure out a style of video I want to make. Look how tiny she is!!! This was something I used to do with my old dog. The scent that we decide on here doesn’t matter. If you have something specific to work on like narcotics then by all means, train with that. I’ve found that it’s pretty easy to introduce new smells later. My last dog could be turned onto a new scent with 2-3 reps of making it super easy. For IGP we are going to need her to use her nose in a different way; however, this is an easy way to work the nose every day.
